title: Defining novel mechanisms of microbiota in regulating anti-tumor responses
text:
Cancer is the second leading mortality in the world, while many different treatments exist including
revolutionary immunotherapies, adverse events are frequent and response rates are limited. Basic,
translational, and clinical studies defined a key role for the gut microbiota in affecting tumor progression and
immunotherapy efficacy, but the underlying mechanism remains at early stage of investigation. The focus of
this proposal is to delineate two novel pathways by which microbiota interacts with mammalian hosts to impact
tumor growth, progression, or immunotherapy response, thus provoking novel opportunities for intervention.

title: Center for Pre-Clinical Cancer Research
text:
Overall
The Center for Pre-Clinical Cancer Research (Cancer COBRE) aims to identify clinically
relevant mechanisms of human cancer disease using models that closely reflect the disease
state in the context of the tumor microenvironment. The four PJI projects feature
osteosarcoma, breast cancer, liver cancer, and prostate cancer as diseases that would
benefit from pre-clinical models that are more predictive of mechanistic efficacy in humans. All
of the PJI projects will use specialized in vivo cancer mouse models and/or in vitro 3D
spheroids to identify relevant mechanisms of tumorigenesis or for evaluation of novel
therapeutic strategies. The Center will promote a unified and coordinated approach by
establishing new specialized core facilities 1) Pre-Clinical Evaluation Core (PCEC) to
provide scientific expertise and technical support for the pre-clinical evaluation and Molecular
Biology and Immunopatholgy Core (MBIPC) to provide access to state-of-the-art
equipment and expertise in Molecular Biology and Immunopathology for the PJI projects.

title: Development and validation of a point-of-need screening test for hepatocellular carcinoma
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide and is frequently
diagnosed at advanced stages, in part due to limited access to effective surveillance tools, particularly in low-
resource settings. This project aims to clinically translate a low-cost, multiplexed point-of-care blood test capable
of measuring a panel of HCC biomarkers with high sensitivity and specificity. By enabling earlier detection in
underserved populations, this technology has the potential to improve clinical outcomes and reduce disparities
in liver cancer care.

title: Sense4Safety Intervention
text:
The proposed research study aims to test the effectiveness of a technology mediated intervention to reduce fall
risk for older adults with mild cognitive impairment. The intervention called Sense4Safety is designed to 1)
identify escalating risk for falls real-time through in-home passive sensor monitoring; 2) employ machine
learning to inform individualized alerts for fall risk; and 3) link older adults with a coach who will guide them in
implementing evidence-based individualized plans to reduce fall-risk. Falls are a significant public health issue
for older adults; therefore, the study is highly relevant to public health.

title: Adaptive and maladaptive repair after kidney injury
text:
One in ten Americans are affected by chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD is a gene environmental disease.
Critical cell type(s) and pathway(s) responsible for disease development remains unknown limiting CKD
understanding and new therapeutics development.

title: Cell Science Imaging
text: The Cell Sciences Imaging Shared Resource (CSI-SR) provides high-resolution, state-of-the-art imaging technologies for studying the molecular and structural organization of cells, tissue, and bio-engineered materials. In addition to the Director, the CSI-SR is staffed by seven full-time staff scientists who have expertise and training in electron and light microscopy. The CSI-SR is organized into three interdependent resources: (1) Fluorescence Microscopy Core (FMC), (2) Electron Microscopy Core (EMC), and (3) the Multiplex and Array Tomography Core (MAC). The CSI-SR provides imaging services to SCI members in two locations across Stanford's campus, the School of Medicine (Beckman Center) and the School of Engineering Shriram Center (Bioengineering). The two facilities house seven advanced imaging systems that provide confocal, deconvolution, 2-photon, lattice light sheet, and super-resolution (SIM, gSTED) fluorescent light microscopy technologies, a bio-AFM as well as two- electron microscopes for biological TEM and SEM imaging. Additionally, the CSI-SR provides access to training and support on advanced software resources for 3D, 4D interactive, volume imaging of data sets (Improvision’s Volocity, Bitplane’s Imaris), as well as advanced deconvolution software packages (SoftWoRx, and SVI Huygens). Image analysis is further supported by the CSI-SR’s image analysis pipeline development service. Members of all programs regularly use the CSI-SR, with the heaviest use coming from the Cancer Biology and Cancer Stem Cells and Cancer Therapeutics programs. In 2020, 35% of users were SCI investigators. The CSI- SR contributed to over 18 cancer-focused publications (5 high-impact). The annual budget of the CSI-SR is $1,340,953, yet the CCSG request is $103,390. Accordingly, the CI-SR leverages extensive institutional support and seeks only 8% from CCSG funds.

title: Ascorbate protects brain after TBI by epigenetic modulation of 5-hydroxymethylation
text:
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major health problem in veterans of all ages. Every year, thousands
of service personnel suffer TBI and there are >300,000 surviving veterans with post-TBI long-term
consequences. The costs of post-TBI acute care, long-term rehabilitation and loss of productive years
are hundreds of millions yearly. The negative impact of this devastating condition on veterans will
increase enormously unless new therapies that can minimize the secondary brain damage during
acute phase after TBI are tested in preclinical animal models and propagated to clinical trials. Vitamin
C (ascorbate) is an FDA-approved and safe compound for human use which is shown to promote
neuroprotection by modifying epigenetics. Hence, we will test the long-term effects of ascorbate
therapy in rodents of both sexes subjected to TBI. The overall goal is to establish ascorbate as a TBI
therapeutic.

title: Metabolic dysfunction from ECM remodeling in diseases of human RPE
text:
Retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have unique metabolic requirements that are perturbed in disease states.
Findings from our studies will provide a framework for understanding how extracellular matrix dysregulation
leads to increased lipid generation and reduced anti-oxidative capacity in human RPE cells. These studies will
expedite the understanding of the underlying causes of RPE-related disease and facilitate treatment discovery.

title: The uncharacterized nuclear protein HMGXB4 in occlusive vascular diseases
text:
Occlusive vascular diseases are the leading cause of death in the United States and worldwide. The proposed
study focuses on investigating the function and the underlying mechanisms of the uncharacterized nuclear
protein HMGXB4 in vascular smooth muscle cells related to occlusive vascular diseases. Completion of the
proposed studies will provide novel insights into the mechanisms regulating smooth muscle inflammation and
phenotypic switching, and will determine if inhibiting HMGXB4 is an attractive novel therapeutic strategy for
ameliorating occlusive vascular diseases.

title: Utilizing Heterogeneous Mouse Models to Discover Mechanisms Underlying Caloric Restriction (CR) on Cognitive Outcomes
text:
Caloric restriction, age, and genetic diversity significantly influence how and when normal cognitive decline and
brain diseases like Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) manifest. This proposal uses a mouse-to-human approach
specifically designed to elucidate genetic mechanisms through which caloric restriction affects cognitive aging
in mice and validates their relevance to humans. This project discovers and leverages genetic factors that
protect the brain in response to caloric restriction to point to new therapeutic strategies for managing or
delaying age-related cognitive decline in the context of resilience to AD.

title: Quantitative chest imaging and serum proteomics in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease
text:
The proposed studies will contribute fundamental knowledge about systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-
associated interstitial lung disease (SARD-ILD), a severe disease manifestation of conditions like rheumatoid
arthritis, systemic sclerosis, and Sjögren's disease. The proposed study will investigate the use of advanced
radiology and blood testing techniques for detection of patients at high risk of SARD-ILD progression. Future
work stemming from these proposed projects may include the development of early detection and treatment
approaches to prevent and slow SARD-ILD disease progression.

title: The Role of Hematopoietic Loss of Y Chromosome on Aging Phenotypes
text:
Many elderly men have a condition where a portion of their blood cells lose the Y chromosome, which may
accelerate aging and age-related diseases, contributing in part to the five-year average reduced life expectancy
in men compared to women. In this proposal, I will investigate how loss of Y chromosome in blood cells promotes
accelerated aging phenotypes through dysregulated immune cell functions leading to increased accumulation of
senescent cells and mesenchymal cell transitions. These findings will identify potential therapies to target
mechanisms of aging that could increase lifespan of men with loss of the Y chromosome.

title: Defining the Function of Age-Related Epimutation in Intestinal Tumorigenesis
text:
Epigenetic modifications to DNA, such as hypermethylation, play a pivotal role in regulating gene expression
during aging and cancer development. By leveraging innovative mouse models and cutting-edge gene editing
approaches, we will elucidate age-related epigenetic changes underlying colon cancer pathogenesis and test
the effectiveness of combination therapy targeting these changes. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel
epigenetic-based strategies for improving outcomes in patients with colon cancer.

title: Mechanisms of Molecular Warfare: Decoding the Arms Race Between Bacteria and Phage
text:
Bacterial viruses (phages) are major drivers of bacterial evolution and encode a vast array of
uncharacterized genes that likely impact bacterial fitness and physiology. Our research aims to uncover
how phage-encoded proteins—such as AcrVA2 and AcrVAIC1—neutralize bacterial CRISPR-Cas
systems, which protect bacteria against phage. By dissecting these molecular strategies, we hope to
reveal new molecular mechanisms that inform the development of next-generation antimicrobials and
biotechnologies.

title: Novel Biomarkers for Predicting and Improving Immunotherapy Response in Lung Cancer
text:
Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and while immunotherapy offers hope, it
only works in less than half of patients and we can't predict who will respond. We discovered an
11-gene pattern that predicts treatment success and identified a gene called PMVK that acts as
a brake on the immune system, which we will develop into a clinical test and explore as a new
drug target to help more patients benefit from immunotherapy.

title: Diffusion Histology Imaging: A Clinical Tool to Non-Invasively Diagnose and Manage Prostate Cancer
text:
Many of the invasive transrectal prostate biopsies performed for PSA screening are unnecessary—50% of the
men undergoing a biopsy do not have prostate cancer. Although biomarkers and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) has been used more often to help better select men for biopsy, these tools are not accurate enough to
replace biopsy. We have developed a new way of analyzing the MRI images called diffusion histology imaging
(DHI) that can accurately and non-invasively diagnose prostate cancer, which has the potential to reduce—if
not eliminate—unnecessary prostate biopsies.

title: Glucose metabolism & skeletal muscle growth
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on understanding how mechanical
loading stimulates muscle growth and glucose metabolism. With a better understanding of how muscle
responds to mechanical signals it may be possible to generate drug therapies that will increase the size
and improve the metabolic health of muscle in individuals with chronic muscle wasting or metabolic diseases,
such as cachexia or type 2 diabetes.

title: Prospective Genetic Risk Evaluation and Assessment (PROGRESS) in Autism
text: The Prospective Genetic Risk Evaluation and Assessment (PROGRESS) in Autism Center at Columbia University will identify and study a population-based cohort of infants with monogenic risk for autism to evaluate the impact of early life identification of genomic risk variants on parent experience, neurodevelopmental trajectories, and prediction of autism diagnosis.

title: Enhancing Rigor and Reproducibility of Translational Nonhuman Primate Models for Genetic and Regenerative Therapies
text:
The overarching goal of these studies is to develop and implement tools and technologies to ensure rigor and
reproducibility of translational nonhuman primate models for precision genetic and regenerative medicine
therapeutics. These studies incorporate highly sensitive in vivo imaging technologies with correlative methods
focused on the immune system to ensure preclinical studies are predictable and provide essential information
for human translation across age groups.

title: Nanotechnology enabled quantitative imaging of dendritic cell anti-cancer vaccines
text:
An effective anti-cancer dendritic cell (DC) vaccine devoid of intolerable immune-related toxicity would be
groundbreaking. Non-invasive imaging in patients suggests an important link between DC to lymph node (LN)
migration and treatment success, yet established clinical and pre-clinical imaging technologies suffer limitations
that preclude systematic studies that link DC vaccine therapy and migration to LN. This project will establish an
innovative nanotechnology-enabled imaging technology called magnetic particle imaging as a powerful tool
enabling systematic studies that link DC vaccine therapy to mechanisms of action, accelerating clinical
translation.
